questions.body: Which resource is shared by all threads of one process?
questions.explanation: Threads of a process share its address space, so the heap, globals, code and open files are common. Each thread keeps its own stack, registers and program counter.
questions.interview_line: Threads share memory, so they are cheap to coordinate but a bug in one can corrupt the others.

questions.body: Which of these are part of the cost of a process context switch? Select all that apply.

options.text: Switching the address space (page tables, TLB effects)
Cold CPU caches after the switch

questions.explanation: A switch saves and restores CPU state, changes the address space and usually leaves the caches and TLB cold for the new process. Nothing is recompiled.
questions.interview_line: A context switch is pure overhead, so schedulers try not to switch more than they need to.

questions.body: Which of these is NOT one of the four necessary conditions for a deadlock?
questions.explanation: The conditions are mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption and circular wait. Allowing preemption of resources breaks one of them, which is why it is a prevention strategy.
questions.interview_line: To prevent deadlock, break any one of the four conditions, most often circular wait by ordering locks.

questions.body: Always acquiring locks in one fixed global order prevents circular wait, and so prevents deadlock between those locks.
questions.explanation: If every thread takes locks in the same order, a cycle of threads each waiting for a lock held by the next cannot form.
questions.interview_line: A global lock order is the simplest deadlock prevention in real code.

questions.body: In round-robin scheduling, what happens as the time quantum grows very large?

options.text: It behaves like shortest job first

questions.explanation: With a quantum longer than any burst, a process runs to completion before the next gets the CPU, which is first-come, first-served. A tiny quantum instead drowns the system in context switches.
questions.interview_line: Quantum size trades responsiveness against switching overhead.

questions.body: Shortest-job-first scheduling can leave long jobs waiting forever. This problem is called ____.
questions.explanation: If short jobs keep arriving, a long job may never be picked. Aging, which raises a waiting job's priority over time, is the usual fix.
questions.interview_line: Any priority scheme needs aging, otherwise low priority work can starve.

questions.body: Which kind of fragmentation does paging with fixed-size pages avoid, and which can it still suffer from?
questions.explanation: Any free frame fits any page, so there is no external fragmentation. The last page of a process is usually only partly used, which is internal fragmentation.
questions.interview_line: Paging trades a little wasted space inside the last page for no external fragmentation.

questions.body: A process touches a page that is valid but not currently in RAM. What happens?

options.text: The process is killed with a segmentation fault
A page fault occurs and the OS loads the page from disk
The TLB loads it with no OS involvement

questions.explanation: The MMU raises a page fault, the kernel finds the page on disk, brings it into a free frame, updates the page table and restarts the instruction. An invalid access is what causes a segmentation fault.
questions.interview_line: A page fault is a normal event for a valid page, and an exception for an invalid one.

questions.body: With 3 frames and LRU replacement, how many page faults occur for the reference string 1 2 3 1 4 2? (Give a number.)
questions.explanation: 1, 2 and 3 fault (3). The second 1 hits. 4 faults and evicts 2 (the least recently used). Then 2 faults again. That is 5 faults in total.
questions.interview_line: LRU keeps recently used pages, so it approximates the optimal choice well.

questions.body: What is the key difference between a mutex and a binary semaphore?

options.text: A mutex has an owner that must release it; a semaphore has no owner
A mutex counts, a semaphore does not
A semaphore only works across machines
There is no difference at all

questions.explanation: A mutex is owned by the thread that locked it and only that thread may unlock it. A semaphore is a signalling counter that any thread can post, so it suits signalling between threads.
questions.interview_line: Use a mutex to protect data and a semaphore to signal events or count resources.

questions.body: A race condition happens when the result of a program depends on the unpredictable timing of threads that access shared data without proper synchronization.
questions.explanation: That is the definition: unsynchronised access to shared state, where the outcome depends on scheduling order.
questions.interview_line: A race is a missing happens-before relationship between accesses to shared data.

questions.explanation: The first fork makes two processes, and each runs the second fork, giving four processes. Each prints one line, so 4 lines.
questions.interview_line: n successive forks produce 2 to the power n processes.
